content: The Hop Tree, scientifically known as Ptelea trifoliata and belonging to the Rutaceae family, is a deciduous shrub or small tree that typically grows to a height of 6 to 8 meters and features a broad crown. It is native to North America, with its range extending from southern Ontario, Canada, southeast to Florida, USA, west to southern California, and south to Oaxaca in southern Mexico. Taxonomy The Hop Tree is most commonly treated as a single species with several varieties. However, some botanists classify it as a group of four or more closely related species: Eastern Hop Tree (Ptelea trifoliata var. trifoliata or P. trifoliata sensu stricto) Florida Hop Tree (Ptelea trifoliata var. baldwinii or P. baldwinii) Western Hop Tree (Ptelea trifoliata var. crenulata or P. crenulata) Narrowleaf Hop Tree (Ptelea trifoliata var. angustifolia, also referred to as P. angustifolia or P. lutescens) The genus name Ptelea is derived from the Greek word for the elm tree, a name Linnaeus transferred to this genus due to the resemblance of its fruit to that of the elm. The species name trifoliata refers to the three-parted compound leaves characteristic of the plant. Description The Hop Tree is often a small tree but can also grow as a shrub with a few spreading stems. It is commonly found as part of the undergrowth in the Mississippi River Valley and thrives on rocky slopes. The plant has thick, fleshy roots and grows well in rich, moist soil. Its juices are acrid and bitter, and the bark is known for its tonic properties. The twigs are slender to moderately stout, brown in color, and feature deep U-shaped leaf scars. The buds are short, light brown, and fuzzy. The leaves are alternate, measuring 5–18 cm in length, and are palmately compound with three (rarely five) leaflets. Each leaflet is 1–10 cm long, sparsely serrated or entire, shiny dark green on the upper surface, and paler below. Western and southwestern forms of the plant have smaller leaves (5–11 cm) compared to the eastern forms (10–18 cm), an adaptation to drier climates. The flowers are small, measuring 1–2 cm across, with 4–5 narrow, greenish-white petals. They are produced in terminal, branched clusters during the spring. The scent of the flowers is subjective, with some finding it unpleasant and others describing it as delightful. The fruit is a samara, approximately 5 cm across, light brown in color, and matures in the summer. The seed vessel has a thin wing and remains on the tree until high winds in early winter. The bark is reddish-brown to gray-brown, with short horizontal lenticels and warty corky ridges. It becomes slightly scaly over time and has an unpleasant odor and bitter taste. The Hop Tree has been used in various Native American herbal medicines for treating different ailments. Specific Features Bark: Dark reddish-brown, smooth, and bitter with an unpleasant odor. Branchlets are also dark reddish-brown, shiny, and covered with small excrescences. Wood: Yellow-brown, heavy, hard, close-grained, and satiny in texture. Winter Buds: Small, depressed, round, pale, and covered with silvery hairs. Leaves: Alternate, compound, and three-parted, dotted with oil glands. Leaflets are ovate or oblong, 3–5 inches long, and 2–3 inches wide, with pointed bases and either entire or serrated margins. They are feather-veined, with prominent midribs and primary veins. When emerging from the bud, they are very downy and conduplicate. Fully grown leaves are dark green and shiny above, paler green beneath, and turn rusty yellow in autumn. Petioles are stout, 2.5–3 inches long, with an enlarged base. Stipules are absent. Flowers: Bloom in May and June. They are polygamo-monoecious, greenish-white, and produced in terminal, spreading, compound cymes. Fertile and sterile flowers are produced together, with sterile flowers being fewer and falling after the anther cells mature. Pedicels are downy. Calyx: Fouror five-parted, downy, and imbricate in the bud. Corolla: Petals are four or five, white, downy, spreading, hypogynous, and imbricate in the bud. Stamens: Five, alternate with the petals, hypogynous. In pistillate flowers, the stamens have rudimentary anthers. Filaments are awl-shaped and hairy, while anthers are ovate or cordate, two-celled, and open longitudinally. Pistils: The ovary is superior, hairy, and abortive in staminate flowers. It is twoto three-celled, with a short style and a twoto three-lobed stigma. Each cell contains two ovules. Fruit: The fruit is a samara, orbicular in shape, surrounded by a broad, many-veined, reticulate membranous ring, and typically two-seeded. It ripens in October and hangs in clusters until midwinter.
